shipped long-line items (Lichess puzzles CC0, 7-ply lines checked by mate claims); no data of our own: that accuracy falls under fatigue is a pattern players report [R]; block size, the at-most-one-more-error rule and the break ideas are first guesses [H]; the learner's log is the evidence

steps.text: In **Long lines late in the session: measure it on yourself** you compared a fresh set with a late set. D2 asks for more: across a two-hour set, the **second half stays flat**. Split the two hours into four blocks of the same size and the same kind of line. The aim is not a perfect fresh block; it is that block four has no more than one error above block three. The app counts answers. It cannot see tiredness.

**When this log means something.** Blocks must be alike (same length of line, new positions) and long enough: six lines per block, about 30 minutes, is a first guess. Counts are small, so one extra error can be chance; trust a pattern over several sets, not one. It fails if you rest or snack only before the last block, or if the lines get easier. Breaks are a change you test, not a given.

steps.title: What a skipped reply costs
steps.prompt: Solve these three positions. Before each one, write which would hurt most if you were tired and skipped Black's reply, and which would not matter.

steps.text: **What changed.** The first two are long lines of 7 plies, each with a tempting rook capture that loses, so a skipped reply costs most there. The third is a short mate in 2 with no reply to skip, so tiredness has little room to show. Position and difficulty differ too, so read this as a prompt to think, not a test.

steps.prompt: Plan the set before you start. This note stays on this device.

fields.label: The fatigue marker I will watch for:

steps.text: **Reading the log.** Per block, write lines tried, first-try errors and the minute you started. As a first rule of thumb [H], call the second half flat if block 4 has at most one more error than block 3. With about six lines per block this is a coarse test: also look at blocks 1 and 2, and trust a pattern over several sets. A rise points to a marker; try one change next set and keep the rest the same.

steps.prompt: Fill this after the set. The answers are my own count, not a measurement. This note stays on this device.

fields.label: Was the second half flat (block 4 at most one error above block 3)?
The one change I will try next set:

steps.text: **Remember.** The goal is a flat second half: across four equal blocks, block four should have no more than one error above block three. Keep the blocks alike in length and kind, and trust a pattern over several sets, since one extra error can be chance. It fails if you rest only before the last block or the lines get easier.
